title: Empty states that sell the next step
metaTitle: Empty states that show the next step
excerpt: The first empty screen is a landing page inside the product. Show the outcome of one action. A tour of the whole system can wait until there is something to tour.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, one path in a wide landscape for an article about the next step.
caption: One road, one car, a destination you can see. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an empty state show?
faqs.answer: Show what this area will hold once the person acts, and give them one action that creates the first object. Use a real example in their language, not a cartoon of the whole product. If they need a prerequisite, say the prerequisite and link it, instead of offering a button that will fail.

faqs.question: Should an empty state include a product tour?
faqs.answer: A tour of every menu teaches the system before the person has a reason to care. Offer the single next action, and let later screens teach the next decision. A short line on what they will get is enough context. A twelve-step coach mark on a blank page is a second product.

faqs.question: How is an empty state different from an error?
faqs.answer: An empty state means nothing is here yet, and the person can create it. An error means something failed, and the person needs to know what to do now. Mixing them, with a cheerful illustration on a failure, makes the product feel like it is not listening. Write them as different sentences.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An empty state that converts is a landing page that happens to live inside the product. The person has arrived in a room with nothing in it. Show them the outcome of one action. Do not teach the whole building before they have a reason to stay.

The first blank screen is often the moment a new account decides whether the signup was worth it. Spend it on a single next step, in the same voice as the page that brought them in.

## The blank screen is a promise, repeated

They just believed something on the way in. A homepage, an invite, a sentence from a colleague. The empty state should repeat that promise in the product's materials. "Your first report will show the Friday numbers without the export." Then a button that creates the report. The illustration, if you use one, should depict that outcome, not a mascot waving beside a metaphor.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) on how long people stay is a useful clock even here. Visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when a page does not show its value, and a clear proposition has to land inside about 10 seconds to earn more time. An empty dashboard of grey boxes spends that window on furniture. A sentence and one action spends it on the job.

Write the sentence in the product's vocabulary, which should already match the marketing site. If the site said "workspace" and the empty state says "tenant," you have introduced a second company at the worst moment. Pick the word the button uses. Repeat it in the heading. A person scanning should be able to say what will exist after they click.

Got Next and Leadly, as public product interfaces, are examples of screens that can be read quickly. An empty state deserves that same scan. One heading. One sentence. One action. Secondary links, if you need them, sit quietly under the action, not beside it as an equal choice.

## One action, with the outcome visible

Name the object they will create. "New project" is weaker than "Start the Q3 launch project" when you know the job, and stronger than "Get started" in every case. The button should say the verb the system will confirm. If the click opens a form, say so in the sentence, and keep that form short. The empty state failed if it only delayed the paperwork.

Show a glimpse of the finished shape when it helps. A faint sample row, clearly marked as an example, can teach the columns better than a paragraph. Do not let the sample look clickable if it is not real data. A person who edits the sample and loses it will not forgive the cleverness. Label it. Offer to replace it with theirs.

If the action has a prerequisite, the empty state should be about the prerequisite. "Connect payouts before you can record a sale." One link, to that job. A button that errors because the prerequisite is missing is an empty state that lied. Check the condition and change the sentence. The screen can still be short.

[WCAG's overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reference for an action people can perceive and operate. The button needs a real name, visible text, and a focus state. An illustration that is the only way to proceed, with no text alternative, fails people who do not see it and people who are in a hurry. Text first. The picture can support it.

## What not to put in the room

Do not put a tour of the whole system on a blank page. Coach marks on empty navigation teach menus the person cannot use yet. They will dismiss the tour to get to the button, or they will finish the tour and still not know which action matters. Teach the next decision on the next screen, when there is an object to point at.

Do not put a video that must finish before the button works. A thirty-second brand film in front of "create" is a tax. If a clip truly helps, put it behind a link: "See a 20-second example." Let the action stay available. People who already know will not forgive a gate.

Do not fill the space with tips about features they do not have. "Did you know you can invite your company" is a second job. Invitations can have their own moment, after the first object exists, when there is something to invite a person into. An empty room with five tips is a brochure. Brochures do not create the first record.

Do not joke at the expense of the blankness. "Nothing here yet, must be nice" reads as the product shrugging. A light tone is fine if the sentence still says what to do. Humor that replaces the instruction is how teams end up with a charming screen and a support ticket.

## Different empties, different jobs

Not every empty screen is the first day. Write them as a set.

- First use: no objects exist. Sell the one creation action.
- Filtered empty: objects exist, and this view hides them. Say how to clear the filter. Do not offer to create a duplicate.
- Search empty: nothing matched. Repeat the query, offer to clear it, and do not pretend the account is new.
- Permission empty: the objects exist, and this person cannot see them. Say who can grant access. A create button they cannot use is a tease.
- Cleared empty: they deleted the last item. Offer undo if you still can, or the same create action, without a lecture.

Each of these can share a layout. They cannot share a sentence. A single component with one hard-coded pep talk will be wrong four times out of five. Pass in the reason. Write the five sentences in the same voice so the product still sounds like one company.

The filtered and search cases are where products accidentally insult a careful user. They did the work. The view is empty because of a control, not because they failed to start. Point at the control. "No invoices in March. You are viewing April." That is a good empty state. It respects the person who already converted, which is the one you most want to keep.

## The words around the button

Heading, sentence, button, quiet secondary line. That is the stack. The heading is the outcome. The sentence is the condition or the benefit in one breath. The button is the verb. The secondary line is for the exception: "You can import a CSV instead," or "This takes about two minutes."

Read it aloud without the picture. If it still makes sense, the picture is allowed to be quiet. If it does not make sense, the picture was doing a job the text refused, and the text should take the job back. Alt text on the image should describe the image, not repeat the heading as a keyword.

Keep the tone continuous with errors and success. Success can be one line: "The project is ready. Invite someone when you want." Error can be one line: "We could not create it. Check the name and try again." The empty state is the third voice in that trio. Write them in one sitting so they do not drift into three brands.

On a Hanabi interface, these lines are part of the design, not a cleanup pass. Figma can hold the empty, the error, and the success next to the happy path. The browser is where you check that the type still works when the sentence is long in German or when the name wraps. Tailwind and a small set of text styles keep the empty state from inventing a new size just because the page felt bare.

## Measure the step, not the illustration

Watch whether new accounts complete the one action, and how long they take. If they stall, read the sentence before you redraw the illustration. A stall on a clear sentence may be a form problem behind the button. A stall on a vague sentence is the empty state itself. Change one thing at a time so you know which line did the work.

Ask three new users to say what they think the button will do, before they press it. If they guess a different object, rename the button. If they ask what a word means, the word is still internal. This test takes half an hour and replaces a week of visual variations that did not touch the verb.

Do not declare victory because the illustration won a critique. Critique the sentence. The picture can be replaced later without changing the conversion, which is the tell. If removing the picture does not change the action rate, the picture was atmosphere. Atmosphere is allowed after the sentence works. It is not a substitute.

Segment the first-day empty state from the later ones in your notes. A beautiful first-run screen can hide a bad search-empty that your long-term users hit every week. The later screen is where trust is kept. Give it the same writing pass. It will never be in the launch screenshots, and it will be on screen more often.

## The limit of a single step

One action will not explain a complex product forever. It does not have to. The empty state only has to create the first object honestly. The next screen can introduce the second decision, with the object now real. A product that tries to teach everything while the database is empty is protecting the team from sequencing the work. Sequence it. First object. Then the collaborator. Then the setting that only matters once data exists.

Some accounts should not see a sales pitch in the empty state. A member invited into an existing workspace should see the work, or a sentence about waiting for access, not a create flow meant for the owner. Check the role before you reuse the component. The wrong empty state is how invited users decide the product is not for them.

When they leave the screen, the email that follows should sound like the same button. That continuity is the subject of [onboarding email that matches the product](/blog/onboarding-email-that-matches-the-product). Read it next if the empty state is clear and the inbox still speaks like a different company.

If you want help writing the first screen so it sells one step and no more, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current empty state and the sentence you wish the user would believe. The call should end with that sentence, or with a smaller one.
